questions.question: What distinguishes a strong validator from a weak validator?
questions.answer: A strong validator is representation metadata that changes value whenever a change occurs to the representation data that would be observable in the content of a 200 (OK) response to GET. [rfc9110#8.8.1] A weak validator is representation metadata that might not change for every change to the representation data. [rfc9110#8.8.1] Strong validators are ideal for comparisons but can be very difficult, and occasionally impossible, to generate efficiently. [rfc9110#8.8.1] Weak validators are easy to generate but are far less useful for comparisons. [rfc9110#8.8.1] A strong validator is unique across all versions of all representations associated with a particular resource over time. [rfc9110#8.8.1] A validator is weak if it is shared by two or more representations of a given resource at the same time, unless those representations have identical representation data. [rfc9110#8.8.1] Strong validators are usable for all conditional requests, including cache validation, partial content ranges, and lost update avoidance. [rfc9110#8.8.1] Weak validators are only usable when the client does not require exact equality with previously obtained representation data, such as when validating a cache entry or limiting a web traversal to recent changes. [rfc9110#8.8.1]

questions.question: What does a Vary header field on a response tell a cache?
questions.answer: A Vary header field in a response tells a cache which parts of the request message, aside from the method and target URI, might have influenced the origin server's selection of the response content. [rfc9110#12.5.5] A Vary header field containing a list of field names tells cache recipients that they must not use the response for a later request unless the later request has the same values for the listed header fields as the original request or the origin server has validated reuse of the response. [rfc9110#12.5.5] A Vary header field expands the cache key required to match a new request to a stored cache entry. [rfc9110#12.5.5] A Vary header field with the wildcard member "*" tells a recipient that it will not be able to determine whether the response is appropriate for a later request without forwarding the request to the origin server. [rfc9110#12.5.5]

questions.question: How is a quality value in a content negotiation header field interpreted?
questions.answer: A quality value in the content negotiation fields is the value of the case-insensitive "q" parameter, which assigns a relative weight to the preference for the associated kind of content. [rfc9110#12.4.2] A quality value is normalized to a real number from 0 through 1, with 0.001 as the least preferred value and 1 as the most preferred value. [rfc9110#12.4.2] A quality value of 0 means that the associated kind of content is not acceptable. [rfc9110#12.4.2] If no "q" parameter is present, the default quality value is 1. [rfc9110#12.4.2] A sender of a quality value must not generate more than three digits after the decimal point. [rfc9110#12.4.2]

questions.question: How does a cache calculate the freshness lifetime of a stored response?
questions.answer: If the cache is shared and the s-maxage response directive is present, the cache uses the s-maxage value as the freshness lifetime. [rfc9111#4.2.1] If the max-age response directive is present, the cache uses the max-age value as the freshness lifetime. [rfc9111#4.2.1] If the Expires response header field is present, the cache uses the Expires value minus the Date response header field value as the freshness lifetime, using the time the message was received if Date is not present. [rfc9111#4.2.1] If no explicit expiration time is present in the response, a heuristic freshness lifetime might be applicable. [rfc9111#4.2.1] When more than one value is present for a given freshness directive, the cache should either use the first occurrence or consider the response stale. [rfc9111#4.2.1] If freshness directives conflict, the cache should honor the most restrictive directive. [rfc9111#4.2.1] Caches are encouraged to consider responses with invalid freshness information to be stale. [rfc9111#4.2.1]

questions.question: What does the s-maxage response directive do, and which caches does it apply to?
questions.answer: The s-maxage response directive applies to a shared cache. [rfc9111#5.2.2.10] For a shared cache, the s-maxage response directive overrides the maximum age specified by either the max-age directive or the Expires header field. [rfc9111#5.2.2.10] For a shared cache, the s-maxage response directive incorporates the semantics of the proxy-revalidate response directive. [rfc9111#5.2.2.10] A shared cache MUST NOT reuse a stale response with s-maxage to satisfy another request until it has been successfully validated by the origin. [rfc9111#5.2.2.10] The s-maxage response directive permits a shared cache to reuse a response to a request containing an Authorization header field, subject to the directive's requirements on maximum age and revalidation. [rfc9111#5.2.2.10]

questions.answer: Under rfc9111#3, a shared cache must not store a response to a request with an Authorization header field unless a response directive is present that explicitly allows shared caching, along with the other storage requirements in that section. [rfc9111#3.5] Under rfc9111#5.2.2.9, the public response directive explicitly marks a response as cacheable and permits a shared cache to reuse a response to a request containing an Authorization header field, subject to the constraints in Section 3. [rfc9111#5.2.2.9]

questions.question: How does a recipient determine the length of a message body in an HTTP/1.1 message?
questions.answer: In rfc9112#6.3, any response to a HEAD request and any response with a 1xx, 204, or 304 status code is terminated by the first empty line after the header fields and therefore cannot contain a message body or trailer section. [rfc9112#6.3] In rfc9112#6.3, any 2xx response to a CONNECT request means the connection becomes a tunnel immediately after the empty line ending the header fields, and the client must ignore any Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding fields in that message. [rfc9112#6.3] In rfc9112#6.3, if a message contains both Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length, Transfer-Encoding overrides Content-Length. [rfc9112#6.3] In rfc9112#6.3, an intermediary that forwards a message containing both Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length must remove the received Content-Length field and process the Transfer-Encoding before forwarding the message downstream. [rfc9112#6.3] In rfc9112#6.3, if Transfer-Encoding is present and chunked is the final transfer coding, the message body length is determined by reading and decoding the chunked data until the transfer coding indicates completion. [rfc9112#6.3] In rfc9112#6.3, if Transfer-Encoding is present in a response and chunked is not the final transfer coding, the message body length is determined by reading the connection until the server closes it. [rfc9112#6.3] In rfc9112#6.3, if Transfer-Encoding is present in a request and chunked is not the final transfer coding, the message body length cannot be determined reliably and the server must respond with 400 Bad Request and close the connection. [rfc9112#6.3] In rfc9112#6.3, if a message has no Transfer-Encoding and has an invalid Content-Length, the message framing is invalid and the recipient must treat it as an unrecoverable error unless the field value is a comma-separated list whose values are all valid and identical. [rfc9112#6.3] In rfc9112#6.3, when an invalid Content-Length value can be parsed as a comma-separated list whose values are all valid and identical, the message is processed using that single value as the Content-Length value. [rfc9112#6.3] In rfc9112#6.3, if a valid Content-Length is present without Transfer-Encoding, its decimal value defines the expected message body length in octets. [rfc9112#6.3] In rfc9112#6.3, if the sender closes the connection or the recipient times out before the number of octets indicated by Content-Length is received, the recipient must consider the message incomplete and close the connection. [rfc9112#6.3] In rfc9112#6.3, if the message is otherwise a response without a declared message body length, the message body length is the number of octets received before the server closes the connection. [rfc9112#6.3] In rfc9112#6.3, request messages are never close-delimited because they are explicitly framed by length or transfer coding, and the absence of both means the request ends immediately after the header section. [rfc9112#6.3]

questions.question: What effect does the HttpOnly attribute have on a cookie?
questions.answer: The HttpOnly attribute limits the scope of the cookie to HTTP requests and instructs the user agent to omit the cookie when providing access to cookies via non-HTTP APIs such as browser APIs that expose cookies to scripts. [rfc6265#4.1.2.6] If a cookie was received from a non-HTTP API and the cookie's http-only-flag is set, the user agent aborts the storage steps and ignores the cookie entirely. [rfc6265#5.3] The HttpOnly attribute is independent of the Secure attribute, so a cookie can have both the HttpOnly and the Secure attribute. [rfc6265#4.1.2.6]
